content: An audiologist is a healthcare professional who specializes in the identification, diagnosis, treatment, and monitoring of disorders related to the auditory and vestibular systems of the ear. They are trained to evaluate and manage hearing and balance problems. Audiologists provide hearing aids, recommend and program cochlear implants, and offer counseling to families when an infant is diagnosed with hearing loss. They also assist late-deafened adults in developing coping and compensation strategies. Audiologists play a role in designing and implementing hearing safety programs for individuals and industries, as well as newborn and school hearing screening programs. They provide custom-fitted earplugs and other hearing protection devices to prevent hearing loss. Additionally, many audiologists work as auditory scientists in research settings. Their training encompasses a wide range of disciplines, including anatomy, physiology, hearing aids, cochlear implants, electrophysiology, acoustics, neurology, counseling, and sign language. Audiologists typically hold qualifications such as a Bachelor of Science (BSc), Doctor of Audiology (AuD), or Master of Science (MS), depending on the program they attended. In the United States, audiologists historically held a master’s degree and the necessary healthcare license. However, since the 1990s, the profession has transitioned to requiring a doctoral degree (AuD) from an accredited graduate or professional program as the minimum standard for practice. All states mandate licensing for audiologists, and they may also obtain national board certification from the American Board of Audiology (ABA) or a Certificate of Clinical Competence in Audiology (CCC-A) from the American Speech-Language-Hearing Association. Audiologists are autonomous practitioners and do not require physician orders or supervision to provide care. However, many work in physician offices or hospital settings. According to the Bureau of Labor Statistics, the median salary for an audiologist in the United States was approximately $78,660 in 2007. Those in the top ten percentile, earning over $98,360 annually, often operate their own private practices.
